_comment: Flow maps, drawn by emtk. Top-level panels are dock windows: the settings on the left, the headline numbers above the field and its profile on the right. The Qt tool's AutoForm spec is flow.view.json.

buttons.label: Map flow
buttons.description: Track each tile's correlation peak and read its velocity. Runs in the background.

buttons.label: Load demo
buttons.description: Simulate a scan whose flow profile is known, and load it, so the arrows can be checked against a number. The first time it simulates the scan, which takes about twenty seconds; later it reuses the file.

buttons.label: Export CSV

sections.label: Image
sections.placeholder: pick a file, drop one here, or load from the database
sections.description: The acquisition to map: a TIFF stack, or a photon stream (PTU/HT3/…) reconstructed into a confocal scan. It needs at least three frames — a flow map measures what moved *between* frames, so a single image carries no velocity at all. If you have never run one, press ▶ Load demo in the toolbar: it simulates a scan whose flow profile is known, so the arrows can be checked against a number.
Pick the acquisition from disk or from the database.

buttons.label: Browse
buttons.description: Browse for an image stack or photon-stream file on disk.

buttons.label: Database
buttons.description: Load a dataset registered in the database; the database resolves it to a local file wherever its object store keeps the data.

sections.label: Channel
sections.description: Image channel to map. Pick the one whose molecules are moving; a structural channel that never changes has no correlation peak to track.

sections.label: Estimator
sections.description: How a velocity is read. STICS tracks how far the correlation peak travels between frame lags: two-dimensional and direct, but blind to a flow too slow to shift the peak at all. Pair correlation asks *when* molecules arrive a distance away: one-dimensional along the fast scan axis, resolved per pixel, and the only one that can report no transport rather than slow transport — which is what a barrier looks like. Neither fits a transport model, so there is nothing to initialise.

sections.label: Tile [px]
sections.description: Side of the sub-region each arrow is computed from — the spatial resolution of the map, and the setting that decides the whole result. Smaller localizes the flow but holds fewer molecules and leaves the peak less room to travel; larger averages distinct flows into one arrow. Several focus waists across is the usual compromise.

sections.label: Frame lags
sections.description: STICS only: correlate frame i against frames i+0 … i+N-1. The peak has to stay inside its tile over that whole range — its displacement is v × lag × frame time ÷ pixel size. Overshoot and the correlation map, being periodic, wraps the peak round to the other side, where a straight line fits a confident velocity pointing the wrong way; such tiles are refused and counted rather than reported.

sections.label: Pair distance [px]
sections.description: Pair correlation only: how far apart the two correlated points are. Too small and the transit time falls below the line period; too large and molecules do not survive the trip, so the peak drowns. Run two distances and check the scaling: a flow peak moves as δ, a diffusive one as δ².

sections.label: Min. quality
sections.description: Arrows below this are not drawn. It is not cosmetic: peak jitter fitted to a straight line always yields a slope, and a slope is a speed, so an unfiltered map paints a convincing flow field onto a sample that has none. Raise it until a region you know is static goes blank.

sections.title: Scanner
sections.description: How the scanner ran: a velocity is a distance over a time, and both come from here, not from the image.

sections.label: Pixel dwell [µs]
sections.description: Time the beam spends on each pixel. With the line and frame times left at zero they are derived from it, which is exact for a scanner without dead time between lines or frames.

sections.label: Frame time [ms]
sections.description: Time between one frame and the next. This is the clock a STICS velocity is measured against, so an inter-frame dead time that is not accounted for scales every arrow. Zero derives it from the dwell.

sections.label: Line time [ms]
sections.description: Time between one line and the next; the clock the pair-correlation lags are measured against. Zero derives it from the dwell.

sections.label: Pixel size [nm]
sections.description: Physical pixel size. Every velocity scales linearly with it, so an uncertain pixel size is an equally uncertain µm/s.

sections.title: Display and estimator
sections.description: Display and estimator details: the arrow length, the tile step and the background removed before correlating.

sections.label: Arrow scale
sections.description: Multiplies the drawn arrow length. Display only — it never touches the numbers, and the caption under the field says what scale was used.

sections.label: Tile step [px]
sections.description: Distance between neighbouring tile origins. Zero uses half a tile, so tiles overlap — which smooths the field without adding information. Set it equal to the tile size for independent tiles.

sections.label: Background
sections.description: 'Each frame's own mean' removes the offset. 'Also the time-average' additionally removes whatever never moves — the immobile fraction — which otherwise adds a correlation peak fixed at zero lag and drags every velocity towards zero. On a sample with genuinely stuck material the difference is large.

sections.title: Flow
sections.description: The headline numbers: mean speed, mean direction, and how coherent the field is. A low coherence with a high mean speed is a structured flow, not a failed measurement.

sections.title: Flow
sections.description: The headline numbers: mean speed, mean direction, and how coherent the field is. A low coherence with a high mean speed is a structured flow, not a failed measurement.

sections.title: Flow field
sections.description: One arrow per tile, over the time-averaged image. Arrow colour runs from cool for the slowest to warm for the fastest tile in this field. Check the direction first: it is the part a correlation measurement gets right even where the magnitude is conservative.

sections.title: Flow field
sections.description: One arrow per tile, over the time-averaged image. Arrow colour runs from cool for the slowest to warm for the fastest tile in this field. Check the direction first: it is the part a correlation measurement gets right even where the magnitude is conservative.

options.empty: Map a file (or load the demo): one arrow per tile is drawn here over the time-averaged image.

sections.title: Profile
sections.description: The field collapsed to one curve: mean speed and mean v_x against position down the frame. A channel flow is parabolic across it — fastest in the middle, zero at the walls — which is the shape to look for. With the demo loaded the simulated truth is drawn beside it.

columns.description: Velocity along the slow scan axis.

columns.description: Magnitude of the velocity, in µm/s.

columns.title: Angle [°]
columns.description: Direction measured from the fast scan axis.

columns.title: Quality
columns.description: Goodness of the straight line fitted through the tracked peaks. A tile with no directed transport still produces a velocity; this is the number that says not to believe it.
